name: Integrity: Process Over Detection
title: Integrity: Process Over Detection
answer: Integrity: Process Over Detection means a school judges writing by how it was made rather than by a detector score. It matters because detection tools can wrongly flag students, especially those learning English, and because a score cannot prove cheating. The alternative is to make the writing process visible through drafts, conferences, in class writing, and marked AI use.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Many schools first bought detection software when AI writing appeared. The text warns that this response is risky because detectors can misread simple writing by students whose first language is not English as machine written. A false flag can turn into an accusation of cheating. The idea of process over detection shifts attention to version history, drafts, conversations, and declared AI use. It solves the problem of trying to prove authorship from a single finished product by looking instead at how the work developed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text describes this approach for kindergarten through 12th grade and does not separate it into narrower grade bands. Teachers can use version history to see how a piece of writing grew over time, and a draft that appears all at once can prompt a conversation. Short writing done in class, brief conferences where students explain their choices, and AI use levels marked on each assignment all make the student's thinking visible. Figure 6.5 brings these practices together. The process becomes part of the grade, so students learn that how they write matters, not only what they hand in.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels the evidence as research that gives strong reasons for caution. It cites a widely cited study finding that tools built to detect AI writing often flagged essays by writers whose first language is not English as machine written when they were not (Liang et al., 2023). It also notes that some detectors perform better, and that one test company built detectors that showed no such bias on its own adult test data (Jiang et al., 2024). The text adds that a school cannot easily know how its own tool behaves with its own students. It states that a detection score should never be treated as proof of cheating, and at most is a reason to look more closely at how a piece of writing was made.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that a detector score is not proof. The text warns that a student learning English could be accused of cheating for writing simply, which is a serious risk of false accusation. Even a tool that performs well on a company's own adult test data may behave differently with a school's own students, so local behavior cannot be assumed. The decision to look more closely, to hold a conference, and to judge the process stays with the teacher and school, not with the software. The text also makes clear that the process approach depends on designed work, visible drafts, and conversations, not on automated verdicts.
